title: Repaying parents
hook: a hundred years on your shoulders isn't enough: two Buddhist answers to what repays a parent
tomorrow: and when a parent is hard to be around?

segments.voice: Yesterday, east: parents are the first direction, and five duties run each way. One of the child's five was supporting the parents who supported them. Today, the question underneath it: can that duty ever be finished?

What could ever repay a parent? Rides, meals, nights up with a fever, small worries kept quiet. People try: a card, a trip, a new couch for the living room. The Buddha's answer starts with an image that sounds like a challenge. Carry your mother on one shoulder and your father on the other, for a hundred years. It still wouldn't be enough.
screen: `WHAT COULD REPAY A PARENT?` → `ONE ON EACH SHOULDER.` → `A HUNDRED YEARS. NOT ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: The sutta keeps going. Bathe them, feed them, even make them rulers of the whole earth: still not repaid. Because parents do so much for their children; they raise them, feed them, show them the world. Then comes the one repayment the Buddha does name. If they lack faith, help them to faith. If they lack virtue, help them to virtue. Stingy, to generosity. Unwise, to wisdom. That repays, and more. Now two voices from inside the tradition. The first stands on this sutta. Carrying parents is love, but it gives them nothing that lasts. Only goodness lasts, so the real gift is helping them toward it, gently, by example as much as by words. The second voice comes from the Ullambana Sutra, read in East Asian and Vietnamese Buddhism. There the monk Moggallana sees his dead mother suffering and can't reach her himself. The Buddha tells him to make offerings to the whole community of monks, and the merit frees her. From that story comes Vu Lan, a festival for parents living and gone; at some Vietnamese temples people pin on a rose, red if their mother is living, white if she has died. This voice says: not every parent will listen to a child. Offerings made in their name reach them anyway, even after death. Both voices agree on one thing. Service alone can't repay. Goodness, shared, is the only coin that counts.
screen: `STILL NOT REPAID.` · `ONE VOICE: HELP THEM TO GOODNESS.` · `ANOTHER: OFFER IN THEIR NAME.` · `VU LAN, A ROSE, RED OR WHITE.` · then, large: `HARD TO REPAY.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers, slowly, things a parent or whoever raised you did that you didn't notice at the time: a ride, a meal, a worry kept quiet. Give each one a breath of thanks. If the people who raised you were hard to be around, count whoever else carried you; the sutta's point holds for them too.
Repaying parents: a debt service can't settle. One voice repays with goodness shared, face to face; another, with offerings made in their name, here or after they're gone.
Worth holding: hard to repay, and goodness is the only coin that counts. Two of eleven, on family.

screen: `DAY 1592 COUNTS.` → `FAMILY · 2 OF 11.` → `TOMORROW: AND WHEN A PARENT IS HARD TO BE AROUND?`

howItsDone: Some Theravada Buddhists honor parents by making merit in their name; in Vietnamese, Chinese and other East Asian Buddhist communities, the Vu Lan or Ullambana festival is a time of offerings for parents and ancestors.

fork.setup: your friend's family celebrates Vu Lan with offerings for their parents and grandparents. you lean toward the sutta's view: help them to goodness yourself. what's the best case for their way?
options: offerings are easier than trying to change anyone's mind.
not every parent will listen; offerings in their name reach them anyway, even after death.
the Buddha said only offerings repay parents, not anything a child says.
fork.reveal: the Ullambana tradition's strongest case: Moggallana couldn't reach his mother, and the merit of the offering did. both voices agree service alone can't repay.

original.note: Pali: grateful, knowing what was done for you; the quality behind repaying parents.

trapdoor: what you thought: you repay parents by taking care of them when they're old.
what it means: care can't settle the debt; the one repayment the sutta names is helping them toward faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom.
what a scholar hears: AN 2.32 (numbered 2.33 in some editions) makes the hundred-years image; the Ullambana Sutra, a Mahayana text, roots the Vu Lan festival in Moggallana's offering for his mother.
guess: a debt to parents that care alone can't settle
a fixed share of income owed to parents for life
a vow to live with your parents until they die

chat.says: made the phở w mom. she teared up, said it tastes like her mom's. how do i pay that back?
options: The sutta says chores alone can't. Sharing goodness with her is the repayment.
Do all her chores for a year. Enough service eventually evens it out.
You don't. In Buddhism, parents' care is their own karma, so nothing's owed.
chat.meaning: The Buddha said even a hundred years of carrying parents can't repay them; helping them toward goodness does. Service alone isn't the coin.

tie.story: The Buddha said carrying parents for a hundred years can't repay them; helping them toward goodness can.
tie.friend: Mai can repay her mom by sharing what's good, like cooking together, not by keeping score.
tie.you: what good thing could you share with someone who raised you?

Ullambana Sutra.meaning: a Mahayana text about offerings that freed Moggallana's mother

Moggallana.meaning: one of the Buddha's two chief disciples

Vu Lan.meaning: a Vietnamese Buddhist festival honoring parents

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 2.32 (Kataññu Sutta; 2.33 in some numberings: carrying mother and father on one's shoulders for a hundred years, bathing them, making them rulers, would not repay them; encouraging them to faith, virtue, generosity and wisdom repays and more than repays)
Ullambana Sutra (Moggallana/Maudgalyayana sees his mother among hungry ghosts and, on the Buddha's instruction, makes offerings to the sangha at the end of the rains retreat to free her)
